subtitle: Who is speaking? The Konjunktiv I in a feature
words.intro: In a good German feature, you can tell exactly who claims what, without a single *he said*. The Konjunktiv I does the work, and *so Wendt* slips in between the commas. It’s how a reporter can stand next to a claim without touching it.

grammar[0].blocks[2].text: *er hätte* where *er habe* is available sounds as if the writer doubted the claim.
grammar[0].fact: In a paragraph in the Konjunktiv I, one *so Wendt* is enough to attribute everything around it. If the verb goes indicative, the writer is speaking again. It’s a shift you could easily miss, and that’s often the point: look for the sentence in which the mood changes.

grammar[1].blocks[2].text: The Konjunktiv keeps a reporter neutral. Then the reporter picks *behauptet*, and everything’s been said. Readers of a good paper will notice. So will the lawyers.
grammar[1].fact: There’s a rule in German newsrooms about direct quotes: the source can ask to read them before printing, and very often does. It’s called *Autorisierung*, and it’s not usual in English-speaking countries. Politicians have rewritten entire interviews this way, and some papers have protested by printing them with the words blacked out.

document.intro: A real milk vending machine on a farm in Germany: twenty-four hours a day, you bring a bottle, or buy one. It’s a very short text. You can read every word of it, and you can also report it: *täglich frische Landmilch, so die Werbung*.
document.fact: Many farms now sell their milk at machines like this, since dairies pay them so little per litre. Raw milk sold this way usually carries a note saying to boil it first. The cow on the side has never been deaf.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Report each claim in the Konjunktiv I.
reading.intro: Vroni has come out to Hof Wendt to write a feature. The farmer, Herr Wendt, says that his cows give twelve per cent more milk if they listen to Mozart. Vroni is taking notes. Timo, her intern, has been sent into the cowshed with the radio.
reading.fact: German quality newspapers still train writers in this form, and readers are used to it. Many cowsheds do have a radio on, for the farmer’s sake if nothing else. The studies on music and milk don’t really agree, and you could report them all in the Konjunktiv I.
